newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea ships powdered milk to N.Korean children.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea ships powdered milk to N.Korean children.

text.p: South Korea said on Friday it had completed loading 300 tonnes of powdered milk onto a ship and was packaging corn for delivery to hunger-stricken North Korea.
"The powdered milk is aimed at helping relieve malnutrition among North Korean children," a National Unification Ministry official said.

A ministry statement said the Belgian-flagged vessel carrying the powdered milk would leave the South Korean port of Inchon late on Friday for arrival on Saturday at the North Korean port of Nampo, near Pyongyang.
"We are also selecting and packaging 50,000 tonnes of corn in China to aid the North through the World Food Programme (WFP)," it said. The corn is due to be delivered in August.
The powdered milk and corn are part of the $16 million in food aid that Seoul has pledged in response to an appeal by the WFP for $95.5 million to stave off famine in the North.
In addition to the government-level aid, the South Korean Red Cross on Friday agreed to double its relief supplies to 100,000 tonnes of food, mostly corn.

The Red Cross organisation, which has shipped about half of the amount, would send the rest by the end of September, under an agreement reached on Friday in a Beijing meeting with its North Korean counterpart.
International aid agencies are also stepping up food appeals for the North, warning of imminent starvation, particularly among young children who are most at risk.
The Rome-based WFP launched a fresh appeal earlier this month for $46 million in food aid for the North on top of the earlier request for $95.5 million.
Washington responded quickly, agreeing to increase its 1997 WFP contribution to $52 million from $25 million.

The United States and South Korea have pledged to consider more aid if international relief groups launch fresh appeals. But they maintain that large-scale assistance must wait until Pyongyang begins peace talks.

Pyongyang has agreed to an August 5 meeting in New York of senior officials from the two Koreas, the United States and China to arrange four-nation talks on a peace treaty to replace the truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
The 1953 ceasefire agreement ended fighting but, technically, not the war itself.
